newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Meister stresses need for EMU convergence.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Meister stresses need for EMU convergence.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Edgar Meister warned on Thursday that the euro would not be as strong as the mark if the convergence criteria in the Maastricht Treaty were interpreted loosely.

In a speech prepared for delivery to a conference in Frankfurt, Meister said that it would be difficult to explain to the German people that the euro will be as stable as the mark if Germany's European partners adopted one-off measures which only gave a show of adequate convergence.
"How can one then explain to the public that the euro will be as stable as the mark," he said.

Speaking at the annual general meeting of the Federal Union of German Money and Valuables Transport Companies, Meister said that a major divergence in fundamentals would make monetary policy decisions more difficult.

"A wide diversification in the fundamental data would make monetary policy decisions more difficult, as, for example, an interest rate decision at the European Central Bank would have a different effect in the individual countries," he said.

Meister warned that doubts about a stability-oriented policy of the ECB triggered by overlarge differences between the participants in EMU would signify a risk premium for the currency union and so lead to higher market interest rates.

Meister insisted that a two-year participation in the European Exchange Rate mechanism is mandatory for membership in EMU. He emphasised, however, that "obviously" participation in the ERM as such is not a sufficient proof of convergence.
Meister's remarks follow recent insistence by German officials that Italy's re-entry into ERM this weekend did not automatically lead to a membership in monetary union in 1999.

Meister also called for automatic sanctions as part of the proposed stability pact if countries run up excessive deficits. Such a pact was necessary to create the basis for stable economic policy, he said.
Meister expressed confidence that it "could be possible" for Germany to meet the Maastricht criteria, even though the road towards that goal was not an easy one.
There was no use in speculating about a possible delay of the start of phase three of EMU, Meister added.
